tier_reason: First-party KeyDB blog (Ben Schermel, Sept 2020) compares KeyDB vs Redis 6 with TLS: 'close to 1 million ops/sec' vs '~130k ops/sec', 'over 7X faster', with memtier and server command lines shown and AWS instance types. There is no CPU model, compiler, build flags or published benchmark harness, so it is first-party with partial methodology: C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: over 7x faster than Redis when using TLS (KeyDB close to 1M ops/s with TLS at 16 server threads vs ~130k ops/s for Redis 6 with TLS); Redis with TLS drops 36% vs single-threaded non-TLS Redis and 61% vs non-TLS Redis with io-threads, while KeyDB shows almost no decline using TLS; latency claimed up to 7x lower
corrections.workload: memtier_benchmark --tls --threads=32 (op mix/key sizes not stated on page, i.e. memtier defaults); client on AWS m5.8xlarge (32 cores), KeyDB/Redis servers on m5.4xlarge; KeyDB --server-threads 16 --server-thread-affinity true vs Redis 6 TLS (no io-threads in its TLS start command)
corrections.caveats: First-party blog benchmark (KeyDB's own team); AWS instance types stated but not the CPU model, compiler, or build flags; memtier op mix and key sizes not stated; Redis TLS run was started without io-threads while KeyDB used 16 server threads; repository has had no commits since April 2024 even though the fork's changes are still substantive vs upstream Redis

notes: Metadata checked via gh: BSD-3-Clause, not archived, 12,504 stars, not a GitHub fork (README calls it 'a high performance fork of Redis', so is_fork_of kept). Latest main commit 603ebb27 has author date 2024-03-21 and committer date 2024-04-04; last_commit set to the committer date. The record's '61% with io-threads+TLS' wording was wrong: the page's 61% is TLS Redis vs non-TLS Redis with io-threads.
